claims.text: Homogeneous noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles form when all metal precursors begin reduction within a narrow time window.
A difference in onset reduction potentials below approximately 0.1 V corresponds to the required narrow reduction-time window.
Temporal alignment of precursor reduction produces simultaneous nucleation and atomic-scale mixing.
Larger reduction-potential offsets cause sequential reduction and early-forming seeds.
Sequential reduction and early seed formation lead to phase segregation.
Changing the ligand environment of one precursor can shift its reduction onset by approximately 0.1 V and align it with the other precursors.
Temporal overlap among individual precursor reduction onsets controls co-nucleation events.
Coincident reduction onsets cause all metals to co-nucleate into single-phase seeds.
Co-nucleation maximizes configurational entropy and yields homogeneous alloy nanoparticles.
A precursor that reduces substantially earlier or later than the others forms separate nuclei or deposits on existing particles.
Separate nucleation or deposition on existing particles drives phase separation or core-shell structures.
The ligand-shifted, onset-matched sample will exhibit a single-phase alloy diffraction pattern with a consistent lattice parameter.
The ligand-shifted, onset-matched sample will exhibit a uniform elemental distribution in STEM-EDX maps.
The unshifted baseline with onset-potential differences above 0.1 V will exhibit multiple diffraction features or peak broadening attributed to separate phases.
The unshifted baseline will exhibit segregated elemental domains.
The proposed mechanism applies to wet-chemical, reduction-driven noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle syntheses in which nucleation is rate-determining.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to high-temperature solid-state alloying or post-synthesis annealing processes in which diffusion dominates.
The critical onset-potential threshold may vary by approximately ±0.05 V with solvent or ligand system.
